title: Counting clicks won’t explain Asia’s e-commerce success
gist: The authors argue that standard e-commerce metrics (transaction volume, internet penetration, mobile use) measure technology adoption but not whether businesses convert that adoption into real organisational value, citing their own research review that found over 50 fragmented theoretical models for measuring e-commerce success, and propose a 'Speed, Spending, Skills' (EBS) framework to better diagnose bottlenecks.

themes.theme: Adoption metrics mask a measurement problem

insights.claim: Standard e-commerce indicators — transaction volumes, internet penetration, mobile use, and the number of businesses selling online — are useful but only tell part of the story, because a country can have strong digital infrastructure and widespread technology adoption while businesses still fail to turn those advantages into sustainable commercial performance.
insights.speaker: Niusha Shafiabady
insights.so_what: Investors/policymakers relying on headline digital-adoption metrics (internet penetration, e-commerce transaction growth) to gauge a market's digital-economy health risk overestimating real commercial capability — due diligence should look past adoption to organisational execution.
insights.locator: Transaction volumes, internet penetration, mobile use

insights.claim: The authors' review of recent e-commerce research found a fragmented picture of how success is measured, identifying more than 50 different theoretical models with four established approaches dominating the field.
insights.speaker: Niusha Shafiabady
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale of measurement fragmentation in e-commerce research (50+ models) — a caution against relying on any single index or ranking to compare digital-economy performance across Asian markets.
insights.quote: more than 50 different theoretical models identified and four established approaches dominating the field
insights.locator: Our study reviewed recent e-commerce research

insights.claim: A business can invest in cloud systems, AI, analytics and digital platforms without fundamentally improving how it operates or the value it creates — technology adoption and digital transformation are not the same thing, since technology poorly integrated into decision-making, customer service, logistics or strategy retains limited value.
insights.speaker: Niusha Shafiabady
insights.so_what: A direct warning against equating capex on digital tools with actual business transformation — relevant for evaluating whether Asian e-commerce/tech spending translates into productivity gains or is largely unproductive adoption.
insights.quote: One of the mistakes businesses can make is to confuse buying technology with digital transformation.

themes.theme: A proposed measurement framework (EBS: Speed, Spending, Skills)

insights.claim: The authors' exploratory EBS measurement model — Speed, Spending and Skills — identifies three broad critical success factors representing system performance, sustained financial investment, and organisational capability, offering a way to move from measuring technology adoption to assessing the actual business value digital technologies create.
insights.speaker: Niusha Shafiabady
insights.so_what: A candidate diagnostic framework (Speed/Spending/Skills) that investors or policymakers could apply to distinguish genuinely transforming digital businesses from those merely adopting technology — though the authors caution it is exploratory, not validated.
insights.locator: Our research on measuring e-commerce success

insights.claim: If two economies have similar levels of digital infrastructure but very different e-commerce outcomes, the real diagnostic question is no longer whether businesses have access to technology, but what they are able to do with it and whether digital investment produces meaningful organisational outcomes.
insights.speaker: Niusha Shafiabady
insights.so_what: Useful comparative-diagnosis heuristic: when comparing two markets' digital-economy performance, look at organisational capability gaps rather than infrastructure gaps first.

themes.theme: Generative AI raises the stakes for measurement

insights.claim: The rapid arrival of generative AI, described as the latest phase in e-commerce's evolution beginning in 2022, creates value through prediction, automation and adaptation in ways that may not be visible through traditional measures such as transaction frequency or technology usage.
insights.speaker: Niusha Shafiabady
insights.so_what: Signals that existing e-commerce measurement frameworks may already be obsolete for capturing AI-driven value creation, implying a coming gap between reported e-commerce metrics and actual AI-enabled productivity gains in Asian digital businesses.
insights.locator: This shift becomes even more urgent

themes.theme: Policy implications: diagnose bottlenecks, not just adoption

insights.claim: Asia does not have a single digital market; businesses operate across very different economic, institutional and regulatory settings, and factors like consumer confidence, digital skills, access to finance and smaller businesses' ability to participate effectively all shape outcomes after technology becomes available.
insights.speaker: Niusha Shafiabady
insights.so_what: Cautions against treating 'Asia' as a homogeneous e-commerce market for investment or policy purposes — country-level regulatory and institutional variation materially affects digital-economy outcomes.

insights.claim: The authors argue policymakers should aim not to create another complicated international ranking, but to give governments and businesses a clearer picture of where real bottlenecks are: if infrastructure is strong but businesses lack digital capability, the answer is training and organisational support rather than more technology investment.
insights.speaker: Niusha Shafiabady
insights.so_what: A concrete policy prescription: diagnose whether the constraint is infrastructure or organisational capability before allocating further digital-economy investment, since the two require different interventions.
insights.quote: Better measurement leads to better questions, and better questions can lead to better policy.
